name: Adam Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What happens on a normal factory shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a seed-bag weighing and sealing machine. I watch the hopper, check the bag weight and pull samples to make sure the seam does not open in transport. I have a vocational machine-operations certificate and enough years here to know the common jams, though I am an ordinary operator rather than a lead. The pay is typical for this job.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What matters at home, and how do you approach new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Leena works at a library, and our grown children live separately. We have a small mortgage and about five months of expenses saved. A few other packing plants are near enough to reach, but openings depend on the season. I use an AI tool now and then to simplify a supplier manual, then compare its answer with the printed settings. I will try a new system after people I trust have used it on a real run. I would like fewer shifts in later years if the household numbers allow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the packing team that quicker paperwork will not weigh a bag or test its seam. We still have to pull samples and keep the scale honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our current wages cover the small mortgage, and five months saved gives us room for a normal setback. I know the bag machine and can keep earning while we work out retirement costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep weighing the first filled bags after a hopper change and test the seam by hand. I would use AI only to clarify a manual word, then check the printed setting before an adjustment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel settled about this picture. It leaves the useful parts of my work in place and gives me time to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What tells you a seam is weak?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The corner lifts when the full bag is turned. I turn a filled seed bag and press the seam before a pallet leaves the line. It is a plain check that catches expensive returns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let AI set the scale?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A tool may explain a calibration term, but the approved weight sheet and a checked test bag decide the setting. I would ask the mechanic before changing it.

say: I would **keep** sample weights and seam checks as paperwork improves.
An **approved** weight sheet still governs scale changes.
think: **Current** wages cover the small mortgage and five months saved helps.
The **familiar** bag line still needs physical checks.
do: **Keep** weighing first bags after hopper changes and hand-testing seams.
**Use** AI only for terms while verifying printed machine settings.
feel: **Settled** with familiar work and time to assess retirement costs.
S0.quote: I turn a filled seed bag and press the seam before a pallet leaves the line.
fieldNote: **Adam** is an experienced average-skill seed-bag machine operator with a vocational certificate and typical pay.

steps.text: Keep weighing filled seed bags and checking seams each run

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the plant which planning duties change first and whether a robot bag stacker is genuinely scheduled later. The crew should see a safe complete run and a written staffing plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A stacker could cut the number of hands on the packing shift, possibly mine. Five months saved would give us search time but not replace the operator wage. Other plants exist, though their seasonal vacancies are uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to observe a guarded stacker trial and compare torn bags with our present count. If the plant offers paid instruction on a new AI weight-alert screen, I would learn it and verify its alerts against test bags. I would apply for a posted local packing-check role only if net pay after travel and hours cover our mortgage and household bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the possible cut to shifts, although I am willing to learn a proven screen. I would not run a stacker after watching one demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you operate the stacker in a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would observe first. An offered recognised funded paid place with supervised stops and lockout would let me practise if it fits my shift. I would wait for a mechanic to sign off my control work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no checking role is posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current wage and check actual seasonal packing vacancies nearby. I would apply only if pay after travel and shifts still cover the mortgage. A nearby gate does not mean a job inside it.

say: I would **ask** for safe trial results and written staffing terms.
**Planning** AI changes before physical bag stacking.
think: A **later** robot stacker may reduce my packing-operator hours.
**Five** months saved gives time but not permanent income.
do: **Request** guarded stacker trial and compare torn bags.
**Learn** offered AI weight-alert screen on paid time against test bags.
**Apply** for posted packing-check work only with mortgage-covering net pay and hours.
feel: **Anxious** about possible roster cuts, open to proven paid instruction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the line AGI may handle orders in 2028, while capable robots weighing, sealing and stacking bags around 2031 could change our hands-on work. I would ask for written pay and redeployment terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a substantial cut to bag-line shifts once robots can run the whole process. I will be 63 then. Leena’s library wage and five months saved would buy us some time, but a smaller household income would make the mortgage and living costs harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would postpone buying the replacement car and put mortgage, food and travel costs on a page. I would ask the plant for written redeployment terms. I would apply for a posted local quality-checking job only if it offers paid supervised safety instruction and net pay after travel and shifts cover our bills; if none exists I would search posted nearby packing work at viable wages and hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the likely wage cut. We have some nearby packing options, but five months of cash cannot finance years without my bag-line shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you repair the robots with your certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The certificate covers this bag machine, not safe robot isolation. I would need an offered funded paid practical course before a maintenance role. I would ask for the duties and wage in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop work at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on a date alone. Leena and I would need written estimates showing retirement income covers the mortgage and bills. Until then I would keep looking for paid work.

say: I would **separate** 2028 AGI orders from physical bag robots around 2031.
I would **ask** for written pay and redeployment terms.
think: I **expect** a substantial bag-line shift cut at 63.
**Five** months saved and partner wages give time but not permanent cover.
do: **Delay** car replacement and list essential costs.
**Apply** for posted quality work only with paid safe training and bill-covering net pay and shifts.
feel: **Anxious** about likely wage cuts, able to search with a modest reserve.
S2.quote: We have some nearby packing options, but five months of cash cannot finance years without my bag-line shift.
fieldNote: **Adam** expects the hands-on risk around 2031 after AGI first changes orders in 2028.
His **five-month** cushion and partner wage allow a measured response, but a substantial operator cut would strain bills.
**Quality** work requires a posting, paid supervised safety training and viable net pay after travel; nearby packing is a separate fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew five years allows a proper paid route into quality or machine maintenance if the plant offers places. AGI changes orders in 2031, and capable robots reach the bag line around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 66 near the robot date. I know bag weights and seams, but do not know how to isolate a moving stacker. I would like to reduce shifts someday, but our mortgage still needs a reliable income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enrol in an offered recognised quality-and-robot-safety course only if funded on paid hours, with supervised stacker isolation and class times I can attend. After qualifying I would apply for a posted local quality role only if net pay after travel and shifts meet our bills. If no paid place opens, I would keep the bag-line wage and check posted nearby packing jobs with enough pay and workable hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel cautiously hopeful about a real course, with some anxiety over the later vacancy. I learn new controls after they have been proven on a full run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the practical course assess?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mechanic should watch me stop and isolate the stacker, then test a full bag and reject a weak seam. I would want more than a video. I need paid hands-on stacker practice with a responsible mechanic beside me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would retirement replace a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if written income figures cover mortgage, food and other costs. We have not calculated that yet. If the numbers are short, I need paid work rather than a hopeful date.

say: I would **ask** for a paid recognised place before 2034 robots.
2031 **order** changes come before physical bag handling.
think: At 66, **bag-line** expertise does not prove safe robot-stacker isolation skill.
**Retirement** is conditional on income covering the mortgage.
do: **Enrol** in offered funded paid recognised course with supervised isolation and attendable hours.
**Apply** after course for posted quality job only with bill-covering net pay after travel and shifts.
If **no** paid place, seek posted packing work with viable wages and hours.
feel: **Cautiously** hopeful about proven training, anxious about a real vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our children ten years gives us time to calculate when we could stop full shifts and to train safely if I still need the bag-line wage. AGI changes orders in 2036, and capable robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 68 at the first date and 71 when robots reach the line. We might have left paid work if the mortgage and living costs are covered by real income. I would not promise to be running the stacker in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request written estimates of retirement income and household costs. If those show I still need wages, I would take an offered recognised funded paid course with supervised stacker isolation on attendable hours, then apply for a posted local quality job only if net pay after travel and shifts cover bills. Without a paid course I would check posted packing jobs at workable pay and hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about income that far ahead, though a decade lets us compare real numbers. I cannot count ten years of warning as a paid course place or wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the children to pay the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They can help us read the figures, but they have separate households. Leena and I need to know what our own income will cover. Family care matters, but a budget needs real numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach before leaving the line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would teach a new operator to turn a full bag and press the seam before packing the pallet. A torn seam is wasted seed and an angry customer. The plain checks deserve to survive the new equipment.

feel: **Uneasy** about uncertain retirement income, willing to compare real numbers.
S4.quote: I cannot count ten years of warning as a paid course place or wage.
fieldNote: **Adam** assumes neither a pension payment nor continued bag-line employment at 71.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most because capable robots could cut bag-line shifts around 2031 while we still pay a mortgage. An offered paid safe course and a posted job with sufficient net wages would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I think seed-bag packing is worth doing carefully even when a machine moves the bags. A torn seam is wasted seed and an angry customer.
